requiredDisclosures: Notice must be in writing and state the specific reason
Notice must include the exact rent owed and period it covers (for nonpayment)
Notice must be served: personal delivery, leave with person of suitable age and mail, or affix to door and mail
14-day rent demand must precede nonpayment eviction proceedings
Landlord must provide Good Cause notice under Good Cause Eviction Law where applicable
NYC: landlord must register rent-stabilized units and file annual rent registrations
illegalReasons: Tenant complained to a government agency about housing conditions
Tenant organized or participated in a tenant organization
Tenant withheld rent due to uninhabitable conditions
Discrimination based on race, creed, color, national origin, sex, disability, age, marital status, sexual orientation, military status, or source of lawful income (includes Section 8 vouchers)
In NYC: evicting rent-stabilized tenant without proper just cause grounds
retaliationProtections: Real Property Law Section 223-b prohibits retaliatory evictions
Retaliation presumed if landlord acts within 60 days of tenant complaint or activity
Tenant may raise retaliation as affirmative defense in eviction proceedings
Tenant may sue for damages, attorney fees, and injunctive relief
goodCauseEviction: Effective 2024: covers most NYC tenants and municipalities that opt in. Requires 'good cause' for non-renewal, limits rent increases to 5% + CPI (capped at 10%). Landlord must provide written explanation for any non-renewal.
notes: New York Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act (HSTPA 2019) significantly strengthened tenant rights
Security deposit capped at 1 month's rent statewide
Landlord cannot collect late fees unless rent is more than 5 days late, capped at $50 or 5%
Unlawful lockouts: tenant can call police and sue for treble damages
NYC Housing Court provides free legal services for income-eligible tenants (right to counsel in eviction proceedings)
Good Cause Eviction Law (2024) may apply — check if your municipality opted in
